title: Antihypertensives & the RAAS
summary: Blood pressure pharmacology: RAAS blockers, calcium channel blockers and vasodilators.

lessons.title: Blood Pressure Physiology

levels.kid:
Your heart is a pump and your blood vessels are like garden hoses. Blood pressure is how hard the blood pushes on the walls of those hoses.

Three things make the push stronger: the pump beating harder or faster, the hoses getting squeezed narrower, and more water inside the hoses.

Your kidneys are the water bosses. When pressure drops, they send out a chain of messenger chemicals called RAAS. The messengers squeeze the hoses and tell the kidneys to keep salt and water. Pressure goes back up.

If pressure stays too high for years, it wears out the heart, kidneys and brain. Blood pressure medicines work by turning down one of those three knobs.
levels.hs:
Mean arterial pressure (MAP) equals cardiac output times systemic vascular resistance. Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume, so pressure rises with a faster or stronger heart, narrower arterioles, or more fluid in the circulation.

The body controls pressure on two timescales. Second to second, **baroreceptors** in the carotid sinus and aortic arch sense stretch and adjust sympathetic and parasympathetic output. Over days to years, the **kidneys** set blood volume by deciding how much sodium and water to keep.

The kidney's main tool is the **renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)**:
- Low pressure, low sodium delivery, or sympathetic β1 stimulation makes kidney cells release **renin**.
- Renin cuts angiotensinogen (made by the liver) into angiotensin I.
- **ACE** (angiotensin-converting enzyme), abundant in lung capillaries, turns it into **angiotensin II**.
- Angiotensin II constricts arterioles and makes the adrenal gland release **aldosterone**, which keeps sodium and water.

Current US guidelines call 130/80 or higher hypertension. Almost every antihypertensive drug blocks one step of this system or one term of the MAP equation.
levels.college:
**Determinants.** MAP ≈ CO × SVR. SVR is dominated by arteriolar radius (resistance varies with the fourth power of radius, per Poiseuille), while preload depends on venous tone and blood volume.

**Renin release** from juxtaglomerular cells is triggered by three inputs: reduced afferent arteriolar perfusion pressure (intrarenal baroreceptor), reduced NaCl delivery sensed by the macula densa, and β1-adrenergic stimulation. Renin is the rate-limiting step.

**Angiotensin II** acts mainly through the Gq-coupled **AT1 receptor**:
- arteriolar vasoconstriction
- aldosterone release from the zona glomerulosa
- efferent arteriolar constriction, which supports GFR when renal perfusion falls
- proximal tubule sodium reabsorption
- facilitation of sympathetic transmission, ADH release and thirst
- cardiac and vascular hypertrophy and fibrosis

The AT2 receptor broadly opposes AT1. ACE is the same enzyme as **kininase II**, so it also degrades bradykinin, which matters for ACE inhibitor side effects.

**Counter-regulators** include natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP), nitric oxide, and prostaglandins.

**Drug map:** β-blockers lower renin release, aliskiren inhibits renin, ACE inhibitors block conversion, ARBs block AT1, and MRAs (spironolactone, eplerenone) block aldosterone. Thiazides reduce volume. CCBs and direct vasodilators lower SVR.

**Compensation** is the reason drugs are combined. A pure arteriolar vasodilator triggers reflex tachycardia (baroreflex) and renin release with fluid retention. That is why hydralazine is paired with a β-blocker and a diuretic, and why NSAIDs, which block vasodilatory prostaglandins, blunt most antihypertensives.
levels.phd:
**Guyton's renal-body fluid feedback.** In Guyton's model, long-term arterial pressure is set where the renal function (pressure-natriuresis) curve intersects sodium intake. Sustained hypertension therefore requires a rightward or flattened shift of that curve. A strong version of the argument holds that any drug lowering pressure chronically must, directly or indirectly, shift the curve back. Vasodilators that do not do so are opposed by sodium retention. The model is debated, because the sympathetic nervous system and vascular remodeling clearly contribute, but it explains why diuretics potentiate nearly every class.

**Feedback loops in RAAS blockade.** Angiotensin II feeds back to suppress renin. ACE inhibitors and ARBs remove that brake, so plasma renin activity rises. With ACE inhibitors, angiotensin I accumulates and can be converted by non-ACE enzymes such as chymase. Over months, aldosterone may drift back toward baseline (**aldosterone breakthrough**). With ARBs, angiotensin II rises and is free to stimulate unblocked AT2 receptors.

**The counter-regulatory arm.** ACE2 converts angiotensin II to angiotensin-(1-7), which acts on the Mas receptor to cause vasodilation and to oppose fibrosis. The balance between the ACE/AngII/AT1 axis and the ACE2/Ang-(1-7)/Mas axis is an active research area.

**Phenotypes.** Plasma renin varies widely between patients. Low-renin, volume-expanded hypertension, more common in older adults and people of African ancestry on average, responds relatively better to thiazides and CCBs than to RAAS monotherapy. Group averages are poor predictors for an individual. Primary aldosteronism (autonomous aldosterone secretion with suppressed renin) is far more common in resistant hypertension than once believed.

**Salt sensitivity** involves WNK kinase signaling to NCC, ENaC regulation and possibly interstitial sodium storage in skin.
levels.expert:
**Confirm before treating.** Office readings mislead. Clinicians use correct technique (seated, back supported, arm at heart level, right cuff size, repeated readings) and confirm with home or ambulatory monitoring. That separates white-coat hypertension from masked hypertension, which carries real risk despite normal office numbers.

**Look for secondary causes** when hypertension is young-onset, sudden, severe, resistant or accompanied by hypokalemia:
- primary aldosteronism (aldosterone-to-renin ratio)
- obstructive sleep apnea
- renovascular disease (fibromuscular dysplasia in young women, atherosclerosis in older patients)
- drugs: NSAIDs, decongestants, stimulants, estrogen-containing contraceptives, calcineurin inhibitors, glucocorticoids, VEGF inhibitors
- pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, thyroid disease, coarctation

**First-line classes** are thiazide-type diuretics, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, and dihydropyridine CCBs. Combination therapy is often started when pressure is far above goal. **Resistant hypertension** means uncontrolled pressure on three drugs including a diuretic; spironolactone is the usual fourth agent (PATHWAY-2), once adherence and measurement are confirmed.

**Neurosurgical angle.** Cerebral autoregulation keeps cerebral blood flow fairly constant across a range of MAP, and chronic hypertension shifts that range to higher pressures. Dropping pressure abruptly in a long-standing hypertensive can cause cerebral ischemia even at numbers that look normal. In a patient with an intracranial mass or hemorrhage, hypertension with bradycardia and irregular breathing (**Cushing reflex**) signals raised intracranial pressure and impending herniation. The pressure there is maintaining cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP = MAP − ICP), so the priority is treating the ICP, not the blood pressure number.

**Pitfall:** bilateral renal artery stenosis (or stenosis to a solitary kidney) makes GFR dependent on angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole. Starting a RAAS blocker can then cause acute kidney injury.

keyPoints: MAP ≈ cardiac output × systemic vascular resistance
Baroreceptors handle seconds-to-minutes; the kidney (sodium and volume) sets long-term pressure
Renin release triggers: low afferent pressure, low NaCl at the macula densa, β1 stimulation
Angiotensin II (AT1): vasoconstriction, aldosterone, efferent constriction, ADH, thirst, remodeling
ACE = kininase II, so it also breaks down bradykinin
Vasodilators provoke reflex tachycardia and fluid retention, which is why drugs are combined

test.q: Mean arterial pressure is approximately equal to:
test.explain: MAP ≈ CO × SVR. Heart rate × stroke volume is cardiac output itself, only one factor.

test.q: Which cells release renin?
test.explain: Juxtaglomerular (granular) cells of the afferent arteriole secrete renin. The macula densa senses NaCl and signals them; the zona glomerulosa makes aldosterone.

test.q: Which stimulus increases renin release?
choices: High NaCl delivery to the macula densa
test.explain: β1 stimulation, low perfusion pressure and low NaCl delivery all raise renin. Angiotensin II feeds back to suppress it.

test.q: Angiotensin II's main vasoconstrictor receptor is:
test.explain: AT1 is Gq-coupled and mediates vasoconstriction, aldosterone release and remodeling. AT2 and Mas broadly oppose it.

test.q: Where does angiotensin II preferentially constrict to maintain GFR when renal perfusion falls?
test.explain: Efferent constriction keeps glomerular pressure up. Remove it with a RAAS blocker and GFR can fall, especially with bilateral renal artery stenosis.

test.q: ACE is the same enzyme as:
test.explain: ACE also inactivates bradykinin, which links ACE inhibitors to cough and angioedema.

test.q: Long-term blood pressure is set mainly by:
choices: The carotid baroreceptors, whose set point stays fixed for years
The kidney's handling of sodium and water
Heart rate set by the SA node pacemaker
Stretch receptors in the aortic arch alone
test.explain: Baroreceptors reset within days; the kidney's pressure-natriuresis relationship sets the long-term level.

test.q: A patient starts hydralazine alone. What compensations are expected?
test.explain: The baroreflex speeds the heart, and renin rises causing fluid retention, which is why a β-blocker and diuretic are added.

test.q: Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin ___.
test.explain: Renin makes angiotensin I; ACE then converts it to angiotensin II.

test.q: Which adrenal hormone, released in response to angiotensin II, makes the kidney retain sodium?
test.explain: Aldosterone from the zona glomerulosa increases ENaC and Na/K-ATPase activity in the collecting duct.

test.q: Which organ makes angiotensinogen?
test.explain: Angiotensinogen is a plasma protein made by the liver.

test.q: Cerebral perfusion pressure = MAP − ___.
test.explain: CPP = MAP − ICP (or central venous pressure if higher). Raised ICP lowers CPP.

test.q: Which drug class commonly raises blood pressure and blunts antihypertensives?
test.explain: NSAIDs block prostaglandins that dilate renal vessels and promote sodium excretion.

kidTest.q: What is blood pressure?
choices: How fast you breathe in and out
How hard blood pushes on blood vessel walls
How big your heart has grown
How much your whole body weighs
kidTest.explain: It is the push of blood against the walls of your blood vessels.

kidTest.q: Which organ is the 'water boss' for blood pressure?
kidTest.explain: The kidneys decide how much salt and water to keep.

kidTest.q: If a hose gets squeezed narrower, the pressure inside...
kidTest.explain: Narrower tubes mean more push, just like squeezing a garden hose.

kidTest.q: Which of these makes blood pressure go up?
choices: More water in the blood vessels
Less salt kept by the kidneys
kidTest.explain: More fluid inside the vessels means more push.

kidTest.q: What pumps the blood around your body?
kidTest.explain: The heart is the pump.

kidTest.q: Why do doctors treat high blood pressure?
choices: It makes you grow much taller
It can wear out the heart, kidneys and brain
It changes the color of your eyes
It makes you sleepy during class
kidTest.explain: High pressure for years damages important organs.

advancedTest.q: A patient on an ACE inhibitor for 1 year shows aldosterone back near baseline. The best explanation is:
choices: ACE inhibitor tolerance at the AT1 receptor, so angiotensin II works again despite the drug
Aldosterone breakthrough via non-ACE angiotensin II generation and other secretagogues such as potassium
Increased bradykinin that breaks down aldosterone, triggering compensatory overproduction
Renin suppression by the ACE inhibitor, which removes the brake on adrenal aldosterone
advancedTest.explain: Chymase and other pathways regenerate angiotensin II, and potassium and ACTH also drive aldosterone. Renin actually rises on ACE inhibitors.

advancedTest.q: Why does ARB therapy raise angiotensin II levels?
choices: ARBs directly stimulate ACE activity in the lung, so more angiotensin I is converted to angiotensin II
Loss of AT1-mediated negative feedback raises renin, and angiotensin II is no longer cleared via AT1 binding
ARBs inhibit ACE2, so angiotensin II can no longer be broken down into angiotensin-(1-7)
ARBs are partly converted into angiotensin II in the liver, which then raises measured levels
advancedTest.explain: Blocking AT1 removes the short-loop feedback on renin. The excess angiotensin II can act at unblocked AT2 receptors.

advancedTest.q: A long-standing hypertensive with a stroke has MAP lowered rapidly to a 'normal' value and deteriorates. Mechanism?
choices: Rebound hypertension after the BP drug wore off, leading to a fresh bleed in the same vascular territory
Rightward-shifted autoregulation leaves cerebral blood flow pressure-dependent at that MAP, causing ischemia
Cerebral vasospasm triggered directly by the antihypertensive drug, sharply raising local resistance
Raised ICP from cerebral vasodilation despite preserved oxygen delivery to tissue
advancedTest.explain: Chronic hypertension shifts the autoregulatory plateau right, so a 'normal' MAP sits below the lower limit for that patient.

advancedTest.q: Which counter-regulatory enzyme converts angiotensin II to angiotensin-(1-7)?
advancedTest.explain: ACE2 produces angiotensin-(1-7), which acts on the Mas receptor to oppose AT1 effects.

lessons.title: ACE Inhibitors, ARBs and Renin Inhibitors

levels.kid:
Remember the messenger chain that squeezes your blood vessels? These medicines cut the chain.

ACE inhibitors stop the machine that makes the strongest squeezing messenger. ARBs let the messenger get made, but they cover up the lock it needs, so it can't do its job. Renin inhibitors stop the very first step.

When the messenger can't work, blood vessels relax, the kidneys let go of extra salt and water, and pressure goes down.

These medicines also protect the kidneys and help tired hearts. One of them can cause an annoying tickly cough, so doctors sometimes switch to a cousin that doesn't.
levels.hs:
Three drug families block the RAAS at different steps:

- **ACE inhibitors** (names end in **-pril**: lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril, captopril) block the enzyme that makes angiotensin II.
- **ARBs**, angiotensin receptor blockers (names end in **-sartan**: losartan, valsartan, candesartan), block the AT1 receptor where angiotensin II acts.
- **Direct renin inhibitors** (aliskiren) block the first step. They are rarely used.

Less angiotensin II action means arterioles relax, aldosterone falls, and the kidney excretes more sodium and water. These drugs also lower pressure inside the kidney's filters, which reduces protein leaking into urine. That is why they are preferred in diabetes with kidney disease. They also improve survival in heart failure and after heart attacks.

Side effects to know:
- **Dry cough** with ACE inhibitors, because ACE also breaks down bradykinin. ARBs rarely cause it.
- **Angioedema**, swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, which can be dangerous.
- **High potassium**, because aldosterone normally helps excrete potassium.
- A rise in creatinine.
- **Birth defects**, so they are avoided in pregnancy.

Doctors do not combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB. Trials showed more harm and no benefit.
levels.college:
**ACE inhibitors** competitively inhibit the zinc metalloprotease ACE. Captopril has a sulfhydryl group and a short half-life. Enalapril and most others are ester **prodrugs** activated in the liver (enalaprilat is the IV active form). Lisinopril is active as given and cleared unchanged by the kidney.

**Hemodynamic effects:** arteriolar and venous dilation without reflex tachycardia (angiotensin II normally facilitates sympathetic tone), reduced aldosterone, and efferent arteriolar dilation that lowers intraglomerular pressure. That last effect causes an expected early creatinine rise and provides long-term renoprotection in proteinuric kidney disease. Survival benefit is established in HFrEF and after MI with LV dysfunction.

**ACE inhibitor adverse effects:**
- dry cough from bradykinin and substance P accumulation
- angioedema, bradykinin-mediated, more frequent in Black patients, can appear years into therapy
- hyperkalemia, especially with CKD, potassium-sparing diuretics or supplements
- first-dose hypotension in volume-depleted patients
- AKI in bilateral renal artery stenosis
- fetotoxicity (renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia), contraindicated in pregnancy
- captopril specifically: rash, taste disturbance, rarely neutropenia

**ARBs** antagonize AT1 and share the hemodynamic and renal benefits, hyperkalemia and fetotoxicity, but cause little cough. They are the standard switch for ACE inhibitor cough. Losartan has a modest uricosuric effect.

**Aliskiren** binds renin's active site, lowering plasma renin activity (whereas ACE inhibitors and ARBs raise it). In ALTITUDE, adding it to ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy in diabetic patients increased hyperkalemia, hypotension and renal events, and the trial was stopped. Dual RAAS blockade with ACE inhibitor plus ARB (ONTARGET) likewise increased adverse renal outcomes without benefit.
levels.phd:
**Enzymology.** Somatic ACE has two homologous catalytic domains (N and C) with different substrate preferences. The C-domain dominates angiotensin I conversion, while the N-domain preferentially cleaves the antifibrotic peptide Ac-SDKP and contributes to bradykinin degradation. Classic inhibitors bind both domains through a zinc-coordinating group: sulfhydryl in captopril, carboxylate in enalaprilat and lisinopril, phosphinate in fosinopril, which is cleared by both liver and kidney. Domain-selective inhibitors have been explored as a way to separate efficacy from bradykinin effects.

**Kinin biology and angioedema.** Bradykinin acting on B2 receptors increases vascular permeability. Its degradation is shared among ACE, aminopeptidase P and neprilysin. Inhibiting several of these at once multiplies risk. Omapatrilat, a combined ACE and neprilysin inhibitor, lowered pressure powerfully but caused unacceptable angioedema and was never approved. That is why sacubitril-valsartan pairs a neprilysin inhibitor with an ARB, never an ACE inhibitor, and requires a washout when switching. DPP-4 inhibitors, which degrade substance P, may add risk on top of ACE inhibition.

**ARB pharmacology.** ARBs differ in how they antagonize. Losartan is surmountable, while its carboxylic acid metabolite (EXP3174) and agents such as candesartan behave insurmountably, owing to slow dissociation. This affects duration more than maximal efficacy. Telmisartan shows partial PPARγ agonism in vitro, of uncertain clinical relevance.

**Feedback.** Every RAAS blocker raises renin concentration. Only aliskiren lowers plasma renin activity, because it blocks the enzyme rather than the downstream products. Prorenin binding to the (pro)renin receptor may signal independently of angiotensin, one hypothesis for why aliskiren did not translate to outcome benefit.

**Fetotoxicity** reflects the fetal kidney's dependence on angiotensin II for perfusion and tubular development in the second and third trimesters, producing renal tubular dysgenesis, anuria, oligohydramnios and its sequelae (pulmonary hypoplasia, limb contractures).
levels.expert:
**Starting and monitoring.** Check creatinine and potassium before starting and again within a couple of weeks. A creatinine rise of up to about 30% reflects the intended drop in intraglomerular pressure and is usually tolerated. A larger rise points to volume depletion, a nephrotoxin, or renovascular disease. Clinicians manage hyperkalemia by stopping potassium supplements and NSAIDs, adding a thiazide or loop diuretic, or using a potassium binder (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) so a mortality-reducing drug can continue.

**The "triple whammy".** ACE inhibitor or ARB plus diuretic plus NSAID removes efferent tone, volume and afferent prostaglandin support all at once, a classic recipe for AKI. Sick-day guidance tells patients to pause these drugs during vomiting, diarrhea or poor intake.

**Angioedema** is an airway emergency. ACE inhibitor angioedema is bradykinin-mediated, so antihistamines, steroids and epinephrine are less reliable than in allergic angioedema. Airway assessment and early intubation by the most experienced operator come first. Bradykinin-pathway therapies have mixed trial evidence. After ACE inhibitor angioedema, clinicians stop the class permanently and use ARBs only with caution. Sacubitril-valsartan is generally avoided.

**Reproductive potential.** Women who could become pregnant need counseling, and the drug is stopped once pregnancy is recognized.

**Perioperative pearl.** Many anesthesiologists hold ACE inhibitors and ARBs on the morning of surgery, because induction can cause refractory vasodilatory hypotension when the RAAS cannot compensate. Vasopressin is often the effective rescue. In neurosurgery, where cerebral perfusion depends on MAP, that hypotension matters.

**Choosing.** Prefer ACE inhibitor or ARB in diabetes with albuminuria, CKD with proteinuria, HFrEF and post-MI. For cough, switch to an ARB. Never combine the two.

keyPoints: ACE inhibitors end in -pril; ARBs end in -sartan; aliskiren is the direct renin inhibitor
ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin: dry cough and angioedema
Shared risks: hyperkalemia, creatinine rise, AKI in bilateral renal artery stenosis, fetotoxicity
Renoprotective in proteinuric CKD; mortality benefit in HFrEF and post-MI
Never combine ACE inhibitor + ARB (ONTARGET) or add aliskiren in diabetes (ALTITUDE)
Neprilysin inhibitor + ACE inhibitor = angioedema risk; sacubitril pairs with an ARB

test.q: Why do ACE inhibitors cause a dry cough?
choices: Mast cell histamine release in airways
Accumulation of bradykinin and substance P
Interstitial fluid building up in lungs
test.explain: ACE (kininase II) degrades bradykinin; inhibiting it lets bradykinin and substance P build up.

test.q: A patient develops cough on an ACE inhibitor. Best switch?
test.explain: ARBs block AT1 without raising bradykinin, so cough is rare.

test.q: Which electrolyte disturbance is most typical of RAAS blockers?
test.explain: Lower aldosterone means less potassium excretion.

test.q: RAAS blockers are contraindicated in:
test.explain: They cause fetal renal dysgenesis and oligohydramnios. The other three are key indications.

test.q: In which condition can an ACE inhibitor precipitate acute kidney injury?
test.explain: GFR there depends on angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole.

test.q: Which drug is a prodrug activated in the liver?
test.explain: Enalapril is converted to enalaprilat. Lisinopril, captopril and valsartan are active as given.

test.q: What did the ONTARGET trial show about ACE inhibitor + ARB combination?
choices: A large mortality benefit over either drug alone
More adverse renal events and hyperkalemia without benefit
Less cough than with an ACE inhibitor alone
Better heart failure outcomes and fewer admissions
test.explain: Dual blockade added harm and no benefit, so it is avoided.

test.q: Which ARB has a modest uricosuric effect?
test.explain: Losartan inhibits the URAT1 urate transporter.

test.q: Unlike ACE inhibitors and ARBs, aliskiren lowers:
test.explain: It blocks renin's enzyme activity, so plasma renin activity falls even though renin concentration rises.

test.q: Why do ACE inhibitors reduce proteinuria?
choices: They constrict the afferent arteriole, cutting flow into the glomerulus
They dilate the efferent arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure
They increase GFR so protein is cleared faster from the blood
They kill damaged podocytes so they can be replaced by new ones
test.explain: Lower glomerular capillary pressure reduces protein filtration and slows kidney disease progression.

test.q: What suffix do ARB drug names share?
test.explain: Losartan, valsartan, candesartan, irbesartan, telmisartan.

test.q: What suffix do ACE inhibitor drug names share?
test.explain: Lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril, captopril.

test.q: Swelling of the lips, tongue and throat caused by ACE inhibitors is called ___.
test.explain: Bradykinin-mediated angioedema can obstruct the airway and can occur years after starting.

test.q: Name the direct renin inhibitor.
test.explain: Aliskiren blocks renin's active site; its use is limited after the ALTITUDE trial.

kidTest.q: ACE inhibitors and ARBs make blood vessels...
kidTest.explain: They block the squeezing messenger, so vessels relax.

kidTest.q: Which side effect can an ACE inhibitor cause?
kidTest.explain: A dry cough is a common side effect.

kidTest.q: If someone gets a cough from an ACE inhibitor, the doctor can switch to...
kidTest.explain: ARBs work on the same chain but rarely cause cough.

kidTest.q: Pregnant people should...
kidTest.explain: They can harm a growing baby's kidneys.

kidTest.q: Do ARBs block the messenger's lock or its factory? (lock/factory)
kidTest.explain: ARBs block the receptor, the lock. ACE inhibitors block the factory step.

kidTest.q: These medicines also help protect which organ?
kidTest.explain: They lower the pressure inside the kidney's tiny filters.

advancedTest.q: Why was omapatrilat never approved?
choices: It was too weak to lower blood pressure meaningfully
Combined ACE and neprilysin inhibition caused excess angioedema
It caused severe hepatotoxicity in early trials
It was teratogenic only, which blocked its approval
advancedTest.explain: Both enzymes degrade bradykinin; blocking both multiplied angioedema risk.

advancedTest.q: A patient has angioedema on an ACE inhibitor. Which is LEAST reliable as primary therapy?
choices: Airway assessment and preparation for intubation
advancedTest.explain: The mechanism is bradykinin, not histamine, so antihistamines alone are unreliable.

advancedTest.q: Refractory hypotension at anesthetic induction in a patient who took an ARB that morning responds best to:
advancedTest.explain: With the RAAS blocked, vasopressin's V1 vasoconstriction is often the effective rescue.

advancedTest.q: ACE inhibitors cause little reflex tachycardia compared with hydralazine because:
choices: They also block β1 receptors in the heart, so the heart rate stays down
Angiotensin II normally facilitates sympathetic transmission, and lowering it blunts sympathetic activation
They activate the vagus nerve directly, which slows the SA node during vasodilation
They raise renin levels, and high renin itself slows the heart rate in most patients
advancedTest.explain: Angiotensin II enhances norepinephrine release and central sympathetic outflow; removing it limits reflex activation.

lessons.title: Calcium Channel Blockers

levels.kid:
Muscles need calcium to squeeze, a bit like a car needs gas to go. The muscles around your blood vessels and in your heart let calcium in through tiny doors.

Calcium channel blockers close those doors partway. Less calcium gets in, so the muscle squeezes less.

Some of these medicines mostly relax the blood vessels, so blood pressure goes down. Others mostly calm the heart, so it beats slower and gentler.

One of them, nimodipine, is used for people who had bleeding around the brain. It helps protect the brain while they heal.
levels.hs:
Smooth muscle in artery walls and heart muscle both need calcium to contract. Calcium enters through **L-type calcium channels**. Calcium channel blockers (CCBs) block these channels, but the two main families prefer different tissues.

- **Dihydropyridines** (names end in **-dipine**: amlodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine, nimodipine) mostly act on blood vessels. They relax arterioles and lower blood pressure. Side effects: ankle swelling, flushing, headache, a fast heartbeat as a reflex, and gum overgrowth.
- **Non-dihydropyridines**, **verapamil** and **diltiazem**, act more on the heart. They slow the heart rate and conduction through the AV node and reduce the force of contraction. They are used to control the rate in atrial fibrillation and to treat some fast rhythms. Side effects: slow heart rate, heart block, constipation (especially verapamil), and worsening of weak-heart failure.

CCBs also treat angina, and they are especially good for angina caused by artery spasm. Amlodipine is one of the most common first-line blood pressure drugs.

A neurosurgery link: **nimodipine** is given after a ruptured brain aneurysm causes subarachnoid hemorrhage. It improves outcomes by reducing delayed brain ischemia.
levels.college:
**Target.** Cav1.2 L-type channels carry the calcium that triggers excitation-contraction coupling in vascular smooth muscle (via calmodulin and myosin light chain kinase) and in cardiac myocytes (calcium-induced calcium release). They also generate the upstroke of SA and AV nodal action potentials. This explains the three main effects: vasodilation, negative inotropy, and negative chronotropy and dromotropy.

**Classes and selectivity:**
- Dihydropyridines are vascular-selective, mainly dilating arterioles (little venodilation). Amlodipine has a long half-life and gradual onset. Immediate-release nifedipine causes abrupt pressure drops with reflex sympathetic activation and is avoided in hypertension and acute coronary syndromes. Nicardipine and clevidipine are IV agents for titratable pressure control.
- Verapamil (phenylalkylamine) is the most cardioselective. Diltiazem (benzothiazepine) is intermediate.

**Adverse effects.** DHP edema arises from precapillary arteriolar dilation that raises capillary hydrostatic pressure. It is not sodium retention, so diuretics help little, while adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB (which dilates venules) reduces it. Gingival hyperplasia occurs with DHPs. Non-DHPs cause bradycardia, AV block and constipation, and they worsen HFrEF.

**Interactions.** Verapamil and diltiazem inhibit CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, raising levels of simvastatin, cyclosporine and digoxin. Combining them with β-blockers risks severe bradycardia and heart block. In atrial fibrillation with an accessory pathway (WPW), AV nodal blockers including verapamil can accelerate ventricular rates and are avoided.

**Indications:** hypertension (DHP), stable and vasospastic angina, rate control (non-DHP), Raynaud phenomenon (DHP), and nimodipine for aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage.
levels.phd:
**State-dependent block explains tissue selectivity.** L-type channels cycle through resting, open and inactivated states. Dihydropyridines bind with highest affinity to the **inactivated** state, at a site accessible from the membrane lipid phase on the pore domain. Arterial smooth muscle sits at a relatively depolarized resting potential, so a larger fraction of channels is inactivated, favoring DHP binding. Cardiac myocytes repolarize fully between beats, so far fewer channels are available to bind. Splice variants of Cav1.2 expressed in smooth muscle may add selectivity.

Verapamil and diltiazem are **use-dependent** (frequency-dependent). They reach their site from the intracellular side through the open pore and bind best to open and inactivated channels, so block accumulates at higher firing rates. That is why they are effective at slowing AV conduction during tachyarrhythmias, where nodal tissue fires rapidly.

**Structural biology.** Cryo-EM structures of Cav1.1 and engineered bacterial channels show DHPs at a fenestration between domains III and IV, acting as allosteric modulators that stabilize inactivation. Phenylalkylamines occupy the central cavity below the selectivity filter. Some DHPs are actually agonists (Bay K8644), and small structural changes can flip the effect.

**Nimodipine paradox.** Nimodipine improves outcomes after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, yet it does not reliably reduce angiographic vasospasm. Mechanisms proposed include effects on microcirculatory constriction, cortical spreading depolarizations and neuronal calcium overload. Clazosentan, an endothelin antagonist, reduced angiographic vasospasm but did not consistently improve function. This dissociation taught the field that large-vessel spasm is only part of delayed cerebral ischemia.

**Toxicology.** In overdose, pancreatic β-cell L-type blockade suppresses insulin release, causing hyperglycemia. The stressed myocardium also becomes insulin-resistant and starved of carbohydrate fuel, the rationale for high-dose insulin euglycemia therapy.
levels.expert:
**Picking the right CCB.** For hypertension, a long-acting DHP such as amlodipine is the workhorse. It is effective across ages and ancestries and pairs well with ACE inhibitors or ARBs (ACCOMPLISH favored that pairing over ACE inhibitor plus thiazide). For rate control of atrial fibrillation in a patient with preserved EF, diltiazem or verapamil works well. In HFrEF, avoid non-DHPs because they worsen outcomes. Amlodipine is neutral there if a CCB is needed for pressure.

**Common traps:**
- Ankle edema on amlodipine: lower the intensity or add an ACE inhibitor or ARB rather than a diuretic.
- Verapamil plus a β-blocker, or IV diltiazem stacked on β-blockade: heart block and profound bradycardia.
- Diltiazem raising tacrolimus or cyclosporine levels in a transplant patient, or statin myopathy from CYP3A4 inhibition.
- Giving an AV nodal blocker to pre-excited atrial fibrillation (irregular, very fast, wide and varying QRS).

**Neurocritical care.** Nimodipine is standard after aneurysmal SAH, given enterally. A frequent problem is hypotension, which threatens cerebral perfusion; the regimen is split into smaller, more frequent administrations rather than the pressure being allowed to fall. Nimodipine is never given IV from the oral capsule contents, a fatal error that prompted safety warnings. Nicardipine and clevidipine infusions are first choices for tight pressure targets in intracerebral hemorrhage and before aneurysm securing, because they titrate smoothly without raising ICP the way some vasodilators can. Clevidipine is carried in a lipid emulsion, so egg or soy allergy and disorders of lipid metabolism are concerns.

**CCB overdose** presents with hypotension and bradycardia, plus hyperglycemia that signals severity. Management uses IV calcium, vasopressors and inotropes, high-dose insulin with glucose, and in refractory cases lipid emulsion or mechanical circulatory support.

keyPoints: CCBs block L-type (Cav1.2) channels: vasodilation, negative inotropy, slowed SA/AV nodes
Dihydropyridines (-dipine) are vascular-selective; verapamil and diltiazem are cardiac-selective
DHP edema is precapillary, not volume overload; an ACE inhibitor or ARB helps more than a diuretic
Non-DHPs: bradycardia, AV block, constipation, worsen HFrEF; inhibit CYP3A4 and P-gp
Nimodipine improves outcome after aneurysmal SAH; never give the capsule contents IV
Overdose: hypotension, bradycardia, hyperglycemia; treat with calcium and high-dose insulin euglycemia

lessons.title: Direct Vasodilators and Centrally Acting Drugs

levels.kid:
There are two other ways to lower blood pressure.

The first way is to tell the blood vessel muscles directly: relax! Medicines like hydralazine and minoxidil do that. The vessels get wider, and pressure goes down. But the body notices and tries to fix it, so the heart speeds up and the kidneys keep water. Doctors usually give helper medicines too.

The second way is to talk to the brain. The brain sends "squeeze!" signals to blood vessels. Clonidine tells the brain to send fewer of those signals. It can make you sleepy, and stopping it suddenly can make pressure jump way up.
levels.hs:
**Direct vasodilators** relax arteriolar smooth muscle themselves.

- **Hydralazine** dilates arterioles. It is used in severe high blood pressure during pregnancy and, combined with isosorbide dinitrate, in heart failure. It can cause a lupus-like illness.
- **Minoxidil** is a powerful arteriolar dilator for very hard-to-treat hypertension. It causes major fluid retention and hair growth. That side effect is why minoxidil is also sold as a hair-regrowth solution for the scalp.
- **Nitroprusside** is an IV drug for emergencies that dilates both arteries and veins within seconds. It releases cyanide as it breaks down.

Because these drugs drop pressure without blocking the body's alarms, the **baroreflex** speeds the heart and the kidneys hold onto salt and water. They are usually given with a **β-blocker** and a **diuretic**.

**Centrally acting drugs** reduce the brain's sympathetic "fight-or-flight" output.

- **Clonidine** stimulates α2 receptors in the brainstem. Side effects: sleepiness, dry mouth, and dangerous **rebound hypertension** if stopped suddenly.
- **Methyldopa** is converted in the brain into a compound that also stimulates α2 receptors. It has a long safety record in pregnancy.
- **Dexmedetomidine**, a related IV drug, sedates ICU and surgery patients while letting them keep breathing on their own.
levels.college:
**Hydralazine** is an arteriolar dilator with an incompletely understood mechanism, probably interference with IP3-mediated calcium release in smooth muscle. It barely affects veins, so orthostatic hypotension is uncommon, but reflex tachycardia, renin release and sodium retention are prominent. It can provoke angina in coronary disease. Hepatic N-acetylation (NAT2) clears it, and **slow acetylators** are prone to drug-induced lupus (anti-histone antibodies). Indications: hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and HFrEF in combination with isosorbide dinitrate.

**Minoxidil** is converted to minoxidil sulfate, which opens ATP-sensitive potassium (K-ATP) channels, hyperpolarizing smooth muscle and closing voltage-gated calcium channels. Adverse effects: profound sodium and water retention, reflex tachycardia, pericardial effusion and hypertrichosis.

**Nitroprusside** donates NO, raising cGMP in both arterial and venous smooth muscle, with onset in seconds and offset in minutes. Breakdown releases cyanide, detoxified by rhodanese with thiosulfate to thiocyanate, which the kidney excretes. Risks: cyanide toxicity (metabolic acidosis, rising lactate) with prolonged high-rate infusion, and thiocyanate accumulation in renal failure.

**Central α2 agonists.** Clonidine and guanfacine stimulate postsynaptic α2A receptors in the brainstem (nucleus tractus solitarius and rostral ventrolateral medulla), reducing sympathetic outflow, heart rate and renin. Abrupt withdrawal causes a catecholamine surge with **rebound hypertension**. Methyldopa is a prodrug converted to α-methylnorepinephrine, a "false transmitter" that acts as a central α2 agonist. It can cause a positive direct Coombs test, occasionally autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and hepatitis.

**α1 blockers** (doxazosin, prazosin, terazosin) dilate arterioles and veins and cause first-dose orthostatic hypotension. In ALLHAT the doxazosin arm was stopped early for excess heart failure, so these drugs are now add-ons, useful when benign prostatic hyperplasia coexists.
levels.phd:
**Hydralazine's mechanistic puzzle.** Despite decades of use, hydralazine's primary target is uncertain. Proposals include inhibition of IP3-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, potassium channel opening, and inhibition of prolyl hydroxylases that stabilizes HIF-1α. Its hydrazine group is reactive. Lupus pathogenesis is linked to slow NAT2 acetylation and to oxidation by neutrophil myeloperoxidase into reactive intermediates, along with DNA hypomethylation in T cells, which is also implicated in procainamide lupus. ANCA-associated vasculitis has been reported as well.

**Minoxidil bioactivation.** Minoxidil itself is weak. Sulfotransferase SULT1A1 produces minoxidil sulfate, the K-ATP opener (acting on SUR2B/Kir6.1 in smooth muscle). Follicular SULT1A1 activity predicts response to topical minoxidil for hair loss, an elegant case where a tissue's metabolizing enzyme determines local drug response.

**Nitroprusside chemistry.** Each nitroprusside anion carries one nitrosyl and five cyanide ligands around iron. Reaction with oxyhemoglobin and sulfhydryls releases NO and cyanide nonenzymatically. Cyanide binds cytochrome c oxidase, halting oxidative phosphorylation, so mixed venous oxygen rises while lactate climbs. Rhodanese capacity is limited by thiosulfate supply, the rationale for coadministering thiosulfate in long infusions. Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin.

**Central sympatholytics.** Clonidine's antihypertensive effect was classically assigned to α2A receptors on brainstem neurons, confirmed in α2A mutant mice where hypotension is lost. A parallel imidazoline I1 receptor hypothesis motivated moxonidine and rilmenidine, claimed to produce less sedation, though the I1 receptor's molecular identity remains contested. Dexmedetomidine is far more α2-selective than clonidine. Its sedation works through α2A receptors in the locus coeruleus, disinhibiting sleep-promoting pathways and producing an arousable state with EEG features resembling non-REM sleep, unlike GABAergic sedatives. That property is exploited in awake craniotomy and in neurological examinations of sedated patients.
levels.expert:
**Using direct vasodilators well.** Hydralazine alone causes reflex tachycardia and fluid retention, so clinicians pair it with a β-blocker and a diuretic. In HFrEF, the hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate combination (A-HeFT) reduced mortality in self-identified Black patients, and it is also used when RAAS blockade is impossible because of kidney failure or hyperkalemia. In pregnancy, IV hydralazine, IV labetalol and oral immediate-release nifedipine are the standard agents for severe hypertension. Minoxidil is a last resort for refractory hypertension, often in advanced CKD, and needs a loop diuretic and β-blocker from the start, with an eye on pericardial effusion.

**Nitroprusside in neuro patients.** It is potent and titratable but has real drawbacks in the brain. It dilates cerebral vessels, can raise intracranial pressure and may cause steal, and it requires invasive monitoring and cyanide vigilance. For intracerebral hemorrhage, ischemic stroke before thrombolysis, or before an aneurysm is secured, nicardipine, clevidipine or labetalol are preferred.

**Clonidine traps:**
- Rebound hypertension after missed tablets, especially in patients who are NPO around surgery. A transdermal patch can bridge.
- If a patient takes both clonidine and a β-blocker and both must stop, the β-blocker is tapered first. Otherwise the clonidine-withdrawal catecholamine surge meets unopposed α vasoconstriction.
- Sedation and bradycardia in older adults.

**Dexmedetomidine** is valuable in neurosurgery. During awake craniotomy for tumors near eloquent cortex, the patient can be woken for language and motor mapping. In the neuro ICU it allows serial neurological exams without respiratory depression. Watch for bradycardia and hypotension, which threaten cerebral perfusion. Its sedation is arousable, so a calm patient may still respond to stimulation, which is useful for exams but not a substitute for deep sedation when ICP control requires it.

keyPoints: Hydralazine: arteriolar dilator; reflex tachycardia, fluid retention, lupus in slow acetylators; used in pregnancy and with nitrates in HFrEF
Minoxidil opens K-ATP channels: severe fluid retention, pericardial effusion, hypertrichosis
Nitroprusside: NO donor, arterial + venous; cyanide (and thiocyanate in renal failure) toxicity; can raise ICP
Clonidine and guanfacine: central α2 agonists; abrupt stop causes rebound hypertension
Methyldopa: false transmitter, used in pregnancy; positive Coombs test
Dexmedetomidine: arousable sedation without respiratory depression; awake craniotomy

lessons.title: Hypertensive Emergencies

levels.kid:
Sometimes blood pressure shoots up super high and starts hurting the body right now: the brain, heart, kidneys or eyes. That is an emergency.

Doctors give medicine through a tiny tube in the arm so they can control it exactly, like a dimmer switch for a light.

The tricky part: they must NOT drop the pressure too fast. The body got used to high pressure, and a sudden drop can starve the brain of blood. So doctors bring it down slowly, step by step, while watching closely.

If pressure is very high but nothing is being hurt yet, it is less urgent, and pills over a few days work fine.
levels.hs:
Doctors separate two situations:

- **Hypertensive emergency:** severely high pressure (often around 180/120 or more) **plus** new organ damage happening now. Examples: confusion or seizures from brain swelling, a stroke or brain bleed, a heart attack, fluid in the lungs, a tear in the aorta (dissection), kidney injury, or eclampsia in pregnancy.
- **Severe hypertension without organ damage** (sometimes called urgency): the number is high but nothing acute is happening. It is treated with pills and lowered over days, not minutes.

In an emergency, patients go to the ICU for **IV drugs that can be adjusted minute by minute**, with an arterial line measuring pressure every beat. Common drugs: **labetalol** (blocks α1 and β), **esmolol** (short-acting β1 blocker), **nicardipine** and **clevidipine** (IV calcium channel blockers), and **nitroglycerin** for heart problems.

The general rule is to lower mean pressure by **no more than about 25% in the first hour**, then gently toward normal over the next day or two. The brain's blood flow control has adapted to high pressure, so dropping too fast can cause a stroke.

The big exception is **aortic dissection**, where pressure and heart rate are lowered fast to stop the tear from spreading.
levels.college:
**Definition.** Hypertensive emergency is severe hypertension with acute target-organ injury: hypertensive encephalopathy or PRES, intracerebral hemorrhage, acute ischemic stroke, acute coronary syndrome, acute pulmonary edema, aortic dissection, AKI, grade III/IV retinopathy, thrombotic microangiopathy, or preeclampsia/eclampsia. The organ damage, not the number, defines it.

**General targets** (absent a compelling condition): reduce MAP by no more than about 25% within the first hour, then toward 160/100–110 over the next 2–6 hours, then to normal over 24–48 hours.

**Compelling conditions change the target:**
- **Aortic dissection:** systolic pressure below about 120 within minutes, with heart rate control first (esmolol or labetalol) to reduce shear (dP/dt). Adding a vasodilator before β-blockade causes reflex tachycardia and can extend the tear.
- **Acute ischemic stroke:** keep below 185/110 before thrombolysis and below 180/105 for 24 hours after. Without reperfusion therapy, pressure is often tolerated up to about 220/120 to protect the penumbra.
- **Intracerebral hemorrhage:** lowering systolic toward about 140 is generally safe; large, rapid or excessive drops are harmful.
- **Severe preeclampsia/eclampsia:** labetalol, hydralazine or nifedipine, plus magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis.
- **Catecholamine excess** (pheochromocytoma, sympathomimetic toxicity): phentolamine or another α-blocker; avoid unopposed β-blockade.
- **Acute pulmonary edema:** nitroglycerin plus loop diuretic.

**Agents:** labetalol (α1/β, avoid in bradycardia, asthma, decompensated heart failure); esmolol (β1, esterase-cleared, ultrashort); nicardipine and clevidipine (DHPs, titratable); nitroglycerin (venodilator at low infusion rates, arterial at higher); nitroprusside (very potent, cyanide risk, raises ICP); fenoldopam (D1 agonist); enalaprilat (unpredictable response, avoided in pregnancy).
levels.phd:
**Pathophysiology: a self-amplifying spiral.** A rapid rise in pressure overwhelms autoregulation and stresses the endothelium. Arterioles develop myointimal proliferation and **fibrinoid necrosis**. Microvascular injury activates coagulation and can produce microangiopathic hemolysis. Meanwhile, pressure natriuresis drives sodium and water loss, so many patients are paradoxically **volume depleted**. That depletion further stimulates renin, angiotensin II and catecholamines, which raise pressure and worsen injury. This is why diuretics are not routine early therapy (except with pulmonary edema) and why cautious volume repletion can help.

**Autoregulation and the brain.** Cerebral blood flow is held constant between lower and upper limits of MAP by myogenic, metabolic and neurogenic mechanisms. Above the upper limit, forced dilation ("breakthrough") produces hyperperfusion, blood-brain barrier disruption and vasogenic edema: **PRES**, often posterior, possibly because the vertebrobasilar territory has sparser sympathetic innervation to resist distension. Chronic hypertension shifts both limits rightward through vascular remodeling. Lowering MAP into what would be normal for a healthy person can therefore fall below the remodeled lower limit and cause ischemia. This is the basis for the roughly 25% first-hour rule.

**Evidence in intracerebral hemorrhage.** Hematoma expansion in the first hours predicts outcome, motivating early pressure lowering. INTERACT2 suggested functional benefit from targeting systolic below 140. ATACH-2, which targeted a lower range of 110–139, found no benefit and more renal adverse events. Later analyses emphasized avoiding pressure **variability** and large drops. The precise target remains debated.

**Pharmacokinetic logic.** In the ICU, context-sensitive offset matters more than potency. Clevidipine and esmolol are hydrolyzed by blood esterases, with offset in minutes regardless of organ function. Nicardipine accumulates with prolonged infusion and its offset lengthens. Labetalol's long, variable effect makes overshoot harder to reverse. In a patient whose cerebral perfusion is fragile, the ability to back off quickly is a safety feature.
levels.expert:
**Workup in parallel with treatment.** An arterial line, fundoscopy, neurological exam, ECG, troponin, creatinine, urinalysis, CBC with smear (schistocytes), and imaging guided by symptoms: CT head, chest imaging, CT angiography if dissection is possible. The diagnosis of emergency rests on finding organ injury. A high number with a headache is not automatically an emergency, and treating the number aggressively in an asymptomatic patient causes harm.

**Matching the drug to the organ:**
- Dissection: esmolol or labetalol first, then a vasodilator if needed, plus urgent surgical consultation for type A.
- Pulmonary edema: nitroglycerin and a loop diuretic; noninvasive ventilation helps. Avoid β-blockers in decompensation.
- ACS: nitroglycerin and β-blockade if no heart failure.
- Eclampsia: magnesium, labetalol or hydralazine, and delivery is the definitive treatment.
- Sympathomimetic crisis: benzodiazepines and phentolamine before any β-blocker.

**Neurosurgical patients:**
- Intracerebral hemorrhage: start lowering early with nicardipine, clevidipine or labetalol, aiming for a smooth decline and avoiding overshoot. Reverse anticoagulation at the same time.
- Aneurysmal SAH before the aneurysm is secured: lower pressure to reduce rebleeding (targets vary by center, often systolic below about 160) while protecting perfusion. After securing, the priority shifts toward avoiding hypotension during the delayed ischemia window.
- Ischemic stroke: permissive hypertension unless reperfusion therapy is planned.
- After craniotomy: emergence hypertension raises the risk of postoperative hematoma, so pressure is controlled tightly.
- Raised ICP: avoid cerebral vasodilators such as nitroprusside and high-rate nitroglycerin. Remember the Cushing reflex, where hypertension supports perfusion against high ICP.

**After stabilization,** transition to oral agents, search for secondary causes (renovascular disease, primary aldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, nonadherence, drugs), and arrange close follow-up.

keyPoints: Emergency = severe hypertension + acute target-organ damage; the organ damage defines it
General rule: lower MAP no more than about 25% in the first hour, then gradually over 24–48 h
Aortic dissection: rapid lowering, β-blocker before vasodilator
Ischemic stroke: permissive unless thrombolysis (<185/110 before, <180/105 after)
Catecholamine crisis: α-blockade first, avoid unopposed β-blockade
Titratable IV agents: labetalol, esmolol, nicardipine, clevidipine, nitroglycerin

test.q: Which IV antihypertensive is cleared by blood esterases with an ultrashort effect?
test.explain: Esmolol (and clevidipine) are hydrolyzed by esterases, so effects end in minutes.

test.q: What is the preferred management of very high BP with no organ damage?
choices: IV nitroprusside titrated in the ICU
Oral agents and gradual lowering over days
IV labetalol to normal BP within an hour
test.explain: Rapid lowering offers no benefit and carries risk.

test.q: Which drug is first-line for acute hypertensive pulmonary edema?
test.explain: Nitroglycerin reduces preload and afterload; a loop diuretic is added.

test.q: In eclampsia, which drug prevents seizures?
test.explain: Magnesium sulfate is the seizure prophylaxis; labetalol or hydralazine lowers pressure.

test.q: Severe hypertension causing posterior brain edema is called ___ (abbreviation).
test.explain: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome.

test.q: Which IV drug blocks both α1 and β receptors and is used in many hypertensive emergencies?
test.explain: Labetalol is avoided in bradycardia, asthma and decompensated heart failure.

test.q: Name an IV dihydropyridine used for tight BP control in intracerebral hemorrhage.
test.explain: Nicardipine and clevidipine titrate smoothly.

kidTest.q: A blood pressure emergency means pressure is very high AND...
choices: something in the body is getting hurt right now
your tummy is feeling super hungry
it happens to be your big birthday
you grew a little bit taller today
kidTest.explain: Organs like the brain or heart are being hurt.

kidTest.q: How do doctors lower pressure in an emergency?
choices: As fast as possible to zero
kidTest.explain: Dropping too fast can starve the brain of blood.

kidTest.q: Emergency medicine is given through...
choices: a tiny tube in the arm
kidTest.explain: IV medicine can be adjusted exactly.

kidTest.q: If pressure is high but nothing is hurt yet, doctors usually use...
kidTest.explain: Slower treatment with pills is safer.

kidTest.q: Dropping pressure too fast can starve which organ of blood?
kidTest.explain: The brain got used to high pressure.

advancedTest.q: Why are diuretics usually not first-line early in a hypertensive emergency (without pulmonary edema)?
choices: They are far too potent and drop the pressure dangerously within minutes
Pressure natriuresis often leaves patients volume depleted, and diuresis further activates RAAS
They raise intracranial pressure by shifting fluid into the brain tissue
They cause dangerous hyperkalemia that triggers arrhythmias in emergencies
advancedTest.explain: Volume depletion drives renin and catecholamines, feeding the spiral.

advancedTest.q: Which trial targeted systolic 110–139 in ICH and found no functional benefit but more renal adverse events?
advancedTest.explain: ATACH-2 found intensive lowering offered no benefit over a standard target.

advancedTest.q: Why is PRES often posterior?
choices: The posterior circulation has more sympathetic innervation, which forces vessels open
The vertebrobasilar territory has sparser sympathetic innervation, so it resists distension less
Occipital cortical vessels have weak autoregulation across blood pressures
Posterior vessels are much larger in diameter, so they carry more of the pressure
advancedTest.explain: Less sympathetic protection allows breakthrough hyperperfusion and vasogenic edema.

advancedTest.q: An aneurysmal SAH patient whose aneurysm was just secured is entering days 4–10. What is the BP priority now?
choices: Maximal BP lowering to prevent aneurysm rebleeding
Avoiding hypotension to protect perfusion during the delayed ischemia window
A continuous nitroprusside infusion to keep BP very low
Stopping nimodipine so the pressure is free to rise
advancedTest.explain: Once secured, rebleeding risk falls and delayed cerebral ischemia becomes the main threat.
